canonical_question: Why does the N-2 material form 'ordered nitrogen complexes' while the O-2 material forms 'ordered oxygen complexes' if the lattice sites are occupied by the same light atoms?

question_variants.question: Why does the N-2 material form 'ordered nitrogen complexes' while the O-2 material forms 'ordered oxygen complexes' if the lattice sites are occupied by the same light atoms?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The paper confirms both N-2 and O-2 form ordered complexes and attributes the difference in peak behavior to the specific element (N vs O), but does not explicitly explain the counterfactual 'why' regarding identical lattice site occupation beyond atomic size/strengthening differences.

answers.answer: Both materials form ordered complexes (N-2: ordered nitrogen complexes; O-2: ordered oxygen complexes). The text suggests larger atomic size of nitrogen leads to higher strengthening, implying a difference in the specific complex interaction, but does not fully detail the 'why' for identical site occupation.
answers.measurement_outcome: Ordered nitrogen complexes observed; larger atomic size of nitrogen (0.75 Å) vs oxygen (0.65 Å).
answers.mechanism: Larger atomic size of nitrogen leads to higher strengthening compared to oxygen.
answers.boundary_limitation: Specific mechanism for identical site occupation preference is not fully detailed.
evidence_spans: For the nitrogen-doped N-2 HEA, an additional low-temperature peak (blue curve) and two high-temperature peaks (green and magenta curves) were also observed (see Fig. 5C ).
The peak height of the additional low-temperature peak is 0.002, and that of the two high-temperature peaks is 0.027 and 0.009, respectively.
Hence, only ~5.3% of all the nitrogen atoms in the N-2 HEA contribute to the formation of ordered nitrogen complexes.
